Idle & Incremental Lovers recommends DO NOT FEED THE VIRUS, one (if not) the best incremental so far this year! [i] Hands down the best game in the particular genre inspired by Nodebuster! Absolutely phenomenal how the game totally reinvents its gameplay at each of the 5 "stages". Smooth, elegant, perfectly paced. It kind of reminds me of 'A Game About Feeding A Black Hole' but with some minor differences. There's nothing wrong with being very similar to another game, right now it has 5 stages with more modes planned in the future, according to the developer. It is very linear, you upgrade one stage's tree and then you continue onto the next stage but you don't bring your upgrades with you, it just sort of branches off into a new tree for each stage. Each stage has its own mechanics and minigames involved, while Stage 5 (the last one) had a combination of all the mechanics combined. There are idler aspects but mostly this is an active play game, you have to be actively involved with killing stuff and healing your stuff to progress. I rather enjoyed this very linear game, the upgrades felt fun and relatively quick to progress. Your workers and soldiers (little units that command themselves) are kind of dumb, they group up together, they mine the same stuff, I wish they were independent besides the soldiers. The workers should go off and mine stuff individually, not all huddle together and mine the same thing. I'm not sure it's worth $6.99 but it is the same price as that other game I mentioned. I'm not exactly sure why they released a supporter DLC, that seems a bit rich. Overall I had a good time - maybe 6.5/10.

DO NOT FEED THE VIRUS - Incremental is a surprisingly addictive idle-inspired game that understands exactly how to make progression feel rewarding. At its core, the game revolves around controlling a strange evolving organism that consumes resources, expands its capabilities, and slowly transforms into a self-sustaining engine of destruction. What begins as a simple clicking and collection system gradually evolves into a chaotic web of automated attacks, chain reactions, and nonstop resource generation. The game embraces the satisfying psychology behind incremental design and builds an experience that constantly rewards players with visible growth and escalating power. The gameplay loop is intentionally simple at first. Players guide the organism around the screen gathering biomass while slowly unlocking upgrades that improve efficiency and unlock new mechanics. Early progression focuses on direct interaction and manual resource collection, but the game steadily introduces automation systems that completely change the pace of play. New upgrades allow the virus to attack enemies automatically, generate chain reactions, deploy orbiting projectiles, and trigger large-scale effects that rapidly spread across the screen. Watching a small and fragile organism gradually evolve into an unstoppable force becomes the game’s greatest source of satisfaction. One of the strongest aspects of the experience is how consistently the progression feels meaningful. Instead of relying only on increasing numbers, many upgrades fundamentally alter the way the game plays. Every new unlock adds another layer to the growing system, encouraging players to experiment with different combinations and optimization strategies. Certain builds focus on aggressive offensive power, while others prioritize passive resource generation or survivability. Because each upgrade changes the gameplay flow in noticeable ways, progression rarely feels repetitive even after extended sessions. The pacing is handled especially well for an incremental game. Many titles within the genre eventually slow down into long periods of waiting, but DO NOT FEED THE VIRUS constantly pushes players toward new milestones and discoveries. Unlocks arrive frequently enough to maintain momentum, and the escalating scale of the effects creates a steady feeling of accomplishment. The game succeeds because it understands the importance of maintaining excitement during progression rather than allowing the experience to become stagnant. Visually, the game uses a minimalist style that works perfectly for its gameplay structure. The clean presentation allows players to easily track resources, attacks, and upgrade effects even as the screen becomes increasingly chaotic. Particle effects, energy beams, explosions, and swarming projectiles gradually fill the environment as the virus evolves, creating a hypnotic visual rhythm that becomes satisfying to watch. The simplicity of the art direction actually strengthens readability while reinforcing the abstract sci-fi atmosphere of the experience. The audio design complements the gameplay surprisingly well. Ambient electronic music and subtle sound effects create a relaxing but engaging atmosphere that fits the gradual escalation of the game. Resource collection, attacks, and upgrade activations all provide satisfying audio feedback without becoming overwhelming. Even during later stages when dozens of systems activate simultaneously, the soundscape remains controlled enough to preserve the game’s strangely calming pacing. Unlike many idle games that eventually play themselves entirely, DO NOT FEED THE VIRUS encourages a more active style of interaction. Players continue moving, positioning themselves strategically, and making constant decisions about upgrades and progression paths even after automation systems become powerful. This active involvement helps prevent the gameplay from becoming too passive or detached. The balance between automation and direct control gives the experience more engagement than many similar titles within the genre. The game also benefits from its focused design philosophy. Rather than stretching progression endlessly with excessive grinding, the developers created a shorter but more concentrated experience where every unlock and mechanic arrives with purpose. The game consistently introduces new systems at a satisfying pace without overwhelming players with unnecessary complexity. This structure makes the experience feel polished and efficient instead of artificially prolonged. One of the most enjoyable parts of the game is watching the various systems begin interacting with each other during later stages. Upgrades start combining into massive chain reactions where projectiles trigger explosions, explosions generate resources, and automated helpers create continuous loops of destruction across the screen. The feeling of carefully constructed systems spiraling into efficient chaos captures the addictive appeal that defines the best incremental games. However, the game is not entirely without shortcomings. The opening stages can feel somewhat slow before the more advanced automation mechanics unlock. Players expecting immediate large-scale chaos may need patience during the early progression. Some interface elements are also fairly basic, and readability can occasionally suffer once the screen fills with excessive visual effects during later sections. The overall scope may also feel smaller compared to larger idle games built around endless progression. DO NOT FEED THE VIRUS focuses on delivering a compact and polished experience rather than an infinitely expanding one. Some players may wish for additional endgame systems, deeper customization, or more extensive long-term content after reaching the later stages of progression. Despite those limitations, the game succeeds because of how effectively it captures the core appeal of incremental gameplay. Every mechanic contributes toward the constant feeling of expansion and escalation that makes idle games so difficult to put down. The combination of satisfying progression, active gameplay, and visually rewarding automation systems creates an experience that remains consistently entertaining from beginning to end. DO NOT FEED THE VIRUS - Incremental may not radically reinvent the genre, but it delivers an extremely polished and enjoyable interpretation of active incremental gameplay. Its rewarding progression loops, escalating chaos, and strong pacing make it an easy recommendation for fans of idle games, optimization systems, and progression-focused experiences. Rating: 7/10

I didn't like this game at all, you are being forced to reset everytime the moment the "fun" begin ... FIVE TIMES !!! Then you start over with different mechanics, nothing overlap, just boring different mechanics. Upgrades are super slow and mostly meaningless till you get a specifc chain and boom suddenly everything dies and you "win" the stage and reset .. Think of it like this, you are extremly weak the entire stage, get the right upgrade > you 1 shot everything > win the stage > progress reset for next stage, you don't even get to have fun as the stage just end and all upgrades are deleted. Most notable at the final stage (5th reset) when you turn from 0 to hero the moment you get the blackhole money upgrade, poof you can skip the entire fight and just win under 15 seconds .. what's the point? Literally from getting 3/4b a round you suddenly get 60b+ and able to afford all the upgrades, its bad design. I guess it may be worth the money to some but I rate it 4/10.
